name: Treaty with the Chippewa, 1854 (Treaty of La Pointe)
nations: Ojibwe (Chippewa) of Lake Superior: L'Anse (Keweenaw Bay), Lac Vieux Desert, La Pointe (Bad River and Red Cliff), Lac du Flambeau, Lac Courte Oreilles, Fond du Lac, Grand Portage, Bois Forte
promises: Article 2: permanent reservations set apart and withheld from sale for the L'Anse and Vieux Desert, La Pointe, Lac du Flambeau, Lac Courte Oreilles, Fond du Lac and Grand Portage bands, with a later reservation for the Bois Forte (Article 12).

Article 11: the Ojibwe would not be required to remove from the homes set apart for them, and those living in the ceded territory kept the right to hunt and fish there until otherwise ordered by the President.

Article 4: for twenty years, $5,000 a year in coin, $8,000 in goods, $3,000 in farm implements, cattle and tools, and $3,000 for education; plus $90,000 for the bands' debts and goods for mixed bloods and young men.
Article 9: an examination of arrears owed under former treaties, with sums found equitably due to be paid as the chiefs directed.

breaches.what: The Commission found the Lake Superior Ojibwe land ceded (Royce Area 332, in northeastern Minnesota) worth $3,250,000 on January 10, 1855, and held the treaty's promised consideration of $813,353.19 so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.

breaches.what: The Ojibwe tribes' fish and wildlife commission states that its member tribes retained hunting, fishing and gathering rights in the treaties under which they ceded land, and that state governments aggressively denied those rights.

compensation: Final award of $2,621,174.58 to the Chippewas of Lake Superior in Docket 18-U (March 30, 1978), after deducting $554,795.57 paid on the claim and $74,029.85 in gratuitous offsets from the $3,250,000 interlocutory award.
today: The reservations set apart in Article 2 are the homelands of the Bad River, Red Cliff, Lac du Flambeau, Lac Courte Oreilles, Keweenaw Bay, Lac Vieux Desert, Fond du Lac, Grand Portage and Bois Forte bands. In Lac Courte Oreilles v. Voigt (7th Cir. 1983) the court held that this treaty did not release the hunting, fishing and gathering rights reserved in 1837 and 1842.

nationVoice.nation: Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission (Ojibwe member tribes)
nationVoice.summary: The tribes say their rights in the ceded territories were retained in the treaties and were aggressively denied by the states.

plain.promised: Permanent reservations for the Lake Superior Ojibwe bands, no forced removal from them, hunting and fishing in the ceded land, and yearly payments in coin, goods, tools and education for twenty years.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1978 that the ceded land in northeastern Minnesota was worth $3,250,000 and that the promised $813,353.19 was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.
plain.today: A final award of $2,621,174.58 was made in 1978; whether it was paid has not been traced. The reservations remain the bands' homelands. A 1983 court held this treaty did not give up rights reserved in 1837 and 1842.

openQuestions: Article 11 hunting and fishing rights in the 1854 ceded territory of Minnesota (the Grand Portage, Bois Forte and Fond du Lac litigation and agreements of the late 1980s) were not researched.
Loss of reservation land after allotment and the boundaries of the Lac Courte Oreilles and Lac du Flambeau reservations, left to be fixed later by the President (Article 2), were not researched.
Whether the Article 9 examination of arrears was carried out and paid was not checked.

Audit 2026-11-08: Articles 4, 9 and 11, the Docket 18-U figures ($3,250,000 at January 10, 1855; $813,353.19 promised consideration; $554,795.57 and $74,029.85 deducted; $2,621,174.58) and the Voigt holding checked and held. The GLIFWC statement is a general one about the region's treaties, not specific to 1854, and is attributed as such.
